nameStory: Say's Phoebe carries the name of Thomas Say, a pioneering American naturalist from the early 1800s who explored the western frontier and described many new species. Like other phoebes, it gets the second part of its name from its distinctive call that sounds like 'fee-bee' or 'phoe-be.' Say would be amazed to know that this western bird now occasionally shows up in New England as a rare vagrant!
description: Say's Phoebe is a medium-sized songbird that belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, known for their habit of catching insects on the wing. This sturdy bird has a grayish-brown back, pale peachy-buff belly, and dark tail that it frequently flicks up and down. It's about the size of a sparrow but with a more upright posture and longer tail. In New England, spotting one is quite special since they're primarily western birds that occasionally wander far from their usual range.

idTips.label: Tail-flicking behavior
idTips.description: Constantly flicks its dark tail downward in a distinctive pumping motion while perched, much more pronounced than most other small birds

idTips.label: Peachy-buff belly
idTips.description: Shows warm peachy or salmon-buff coloring on the lower belly and under the tail, especially noticeable in good light

idTips.label: Upright perching
idTips.description: Sits very upright on exposed perches like fence posts or dead branches, with alert posture and frequently turning its head to scan for insects

idTips.label: Grayish-brown upperparts
idTips.description: Back and wings appear dusty grayish-brown without distinct markings, giving it a somewhat plain appearance from above

idTips.label: Dark cap and eye line
idTips.description: Head shows darker grayish coloring that contrasts with the paler throat, creating a subtle capped appearance

habitat: In New England, Say's Phoebes are extremely rare visitors that typically show up in open areas like fields, farmland, or coastal areas with scattered perches. When they do appear, look for them in habitats similar to those preferred by Eastern Phoebes - near buildings, bridges, or open areas with good insect-hunting opportunities. They favor spots with prominent perches like fence posts, utility wires, or dead snags.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring vagrant, most likely to appear during migration periods in April or May. Any phoebe-like bird with peachy underparts during spring migration deserves careful study.
seasonality.summer: Extremely unlikely in summer, though breeding-season wanderers could theoretically appear. Would likely be associated with open agricultural areas if present.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration brings the highest chance of seeing vagrant Say's Phoebes in New England, particularly September through October when western birds sometimes wander eastward.
seasonality.winter: Essentially absent in winter, as Say's Phoebes migrate to warmer regions and would be extremely unlikely to survive New England's cold season.

funFact: Say's Phoebes are such devoted homebodies that they often return to the exact same nesting site year after year, sometimes reusing the same nest cup and even adding new layers on top of old ones, creating apartment-building-style structures that can last for decades!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Eastern Phoebe, but Say's Phoebe has that distinctive peachy-buff belly color instead of the Eastern's white belly, plus a slightly grayer overall appearance. Remember: 'Say's is peachy' for the warmer underpart coloring that sets it apart from our common Eastern Phoebe.
contextualKnowledge: Say's Phoebe sightings in New England are significant enough that they should be reported to eBird and local birding communities, as they represent notable range extensions. These western wanderers help scientists understand bird migration patterns and climate change effects on species distributions.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Eastern Phoebe, Say's Phoebe shows warmer peachy-buff underparts instead of white, and has a grayer overall appearance rather than the Eastern's brownish tones. Both species share the characteristic tail-flicking behavior and upright posture, but the peachy belly color is the dead giveaway for Say's. Eastern Phoebes also prefer areas near water more than Say's Phoebes do.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Eastern Phoebe is the only phoebe species regularly found in New England, making it unique among its genus in our region.
